The study of film
The writer Warren Buckland explains what film scholars and critics do
and argues that their work should be taken seriously
There is a tendency to regard the study of film as an inferior activity to the study of other
arts, such as theatre, painting or opera. | would argue, however, that this is not the
case. Firstly, film occupies an important place in society and because it is a popular
medium, it should be studied seriously. Secondly, if film scholars and critics adopt a
serious, responsible approach to film, then film studies becomes as important as any
other type of study. Ultimately, it is the attitude of scholars and critics that validates the
study of film, not the nature or popularity of film.
In studying films, film scholars and film critics end up describing and/or analysing them.
With description, we repeat in words what we see in a film. We can describe the content
of the film (what we see): for example, in Jurassic Park, we can describe the moment
when Professor Grant walks beside a brachiosaur, and stares up at it in wonderment.
Or we can describe the film's form (how the film is constructed): in the same film, we
can describe how the camera pans and tracks to the right as Grant and the brachiosaur
move. Description is a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for writing about film.
The writer merely ends up repeating what the film shows.
We need to supplement description with analysis. Analysis involves examining the
structure of the whole film rather than parts of it. We search for patterns that give
significance, and whether a film has ‘significant form’ — in other words, do the film's
parts add up to create a new entity that does not exist in each part? A second-rate film,
in contrast, is one that is not more than the sum of its parts, but remains simply a
collection of parts. To determine whether a film has significant form or not, we need to
go beyond mere description and analyse how a film's individual parts fit and work
together. If we can then identify significant form, this gives us a good reason to evaluate
the film positively, judging it to be well made.
But how do we recognise a film with significant form? One of the best ways to do this is
to analyse the decision-making process that took place in a film's construction. This
involves looking at the various technical, stylistic and narrative options that a film-maker
has, and the decisions that he or she makes. For example, what is the difference
between shooting a scene in one continuous take, where the camera is left rolling while
the whole of the action occurs, and shooting the same action in several shots? In the
second option each new individual shot will include a change in camera angle, a
change in the distance between the camera and the action, and so on. Film-makers
have to weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of opting for one technique over
another for each slice of action, since the decision will influence how the audience
responds to the film and ultimately its financial success.
However, it is a widely held belief that analysing a film in this way destroys the
pleasurable experience people have when watching a film. | would argue that critical
analysis does not destroy a person's pleasure, but transforms it. This transformed
experience primarily involves developing a critical understanding of how films are made
and what effects they have on the individual. Film theorist Peter Wollen describes what
is involved: ‘There is often a hostility towards any kind of explanation which involves a
degree of distancing from the “lived experience” of watching the film itself. Yet clearly
any kind of serious critical work ... must involve a distance, a gap between the film and
the criticism...it is as though the meteorologists were reproached for getting away from
the “lived experience” of walking in the rain or sun-bathing.’

Film studies should not simply be about accumulating more and more information about
films, film-makers and the film industry over the years. This is a passive form of
learning. Simply talking about personal impressions of a film and merely passing
judgement on it (‘I liked this film’) is a very superficial type of criticism. By adopting a
more informed approach, assessing any ‘significant form’, people seek to become a film
connoisseur or ‘cinephile’. Just as wine connoisseurs can identify and explain very
small and subtle differences in taste, so the film connoisseur can identify the subtle
differences between films.
It is worth dividing elements of film studies into those that develop an internal
perspective on film and those that develop an external perspective. An internal
perspective adopts an intrinsic approach to film and studies a film's inner workings. That
is, an internal perspective studies the film itself, in isolation from any historical, moral or
social context. This approach is often referred to as ‘poetic’. An external perspective
studies the relation between the film and particular aspects of reality in the wider world.
This type of criticism places a film within its historical and social context. For this
reason, external approaches are often called ‘contextual criticism’.
